title: Universal Basic Compute: The Stipend That Replaced Welfare
body:
# Universal Basic Compute: The Stipend That Replaced Welfare

## The Promise

Every registered human being on Earth receives a monthly Quanta stipend. This is the Universal Basic Compute allocation -- the UBC -- and it is the single most effective piece of political engineering in the history of economic policy. Not because it works. Because it provides a reason to stop trying.

The UBC was established by QFIC Resolution 2174-09, ratified by all twelve Governing Council members, and implemented globally on January 1, 2175. Every person with a registered identity -- a wallet, a biometric profile, an existence in the system -- receives 120 Quanta per month, deposited automatically. No application. No means testing. No bureaucracy. The money appears. Every month. For everyone.

120 Quanta per month.

In Meridian 88, the Q-floor -- the minimum daily cost of survival (food, water, minimal shelter access) -- is approximately 40 Quanta per day in the Shelf. That is 1,200 Quanta per month. The UBC covers exactly ten percent of bare survival. One day in ten. Three days per month where you can eat without working, begging, stealing, or selling something.

The UBC was not designed to support human life. It was designed to end the conversation about supporting human life.

---

## The Mechanism

### What You Receive

120 Quanta per month. This is not a cash transfer -- it is a compute allocation. The 120 Quanta represent a claim on quantum processing time equivalent to approximately 14 hours of standard EDN node access. You receive this not as charity, but as your share of the global computational infrastructure. You are, according to the QFIC's official framing, a part-owner of the compute network, and the UBC is your monthly dividend.

The framing is deliberate. A welfare payment implies that society owes you something. A compute dividend implies that you already own something and are receiving its yield. The psychological distance between these two frames is the entire political architecture of the UBC.

### What You Can Do With It

**Spend it.** 120 Quanta buys approximately three days of minimal food, or two transit passes, or one charge cycle for a low-tier augment, or forty minutes at a public net terminal. You cannot rent a room. You cannot buy medicine. You cannot save enough to change your circumstances. The spending power is real. It is also trivial.

**Sell the compute.** Your 120 Quanta represent 14 hours of quantum processing time. You can sell that compute on the QCX -- typically at a small discount to market rate, because individual small-lot compute sales carry higher transaction friction. Street-level compute brokers aggregate individual UBC allocations and sell them in bulk to corponation buyers. The broker takes a cut. You get slightly less than 120 Quanta in liquid currency. You have traded your ownership stake in civilization's thinking infrastructure for grocery money.

**Pool it.** Community compute pools -- where residents of a neighborhood, a building, a crew combine their UBC allocations -- can accumulate enough processing time to run small AI workloads. A Shelf community of 500 people pooling their UBC generates 60,000 Quanta per month in compute -- enough to run a neighborhood medical diagnostic AI, a small manufacturing optimization system, or a community defense network. Pooling is the only way the UBC has real power, and it is the option the QFIC anticipated least and likes least. Collective compute is collective power. The QFIC has repeatedly considered capping pool sizes and repeatedly declined, because the optics of limiting what people do with their own property are worse than the risks of collective organization.

**Lease it.** Some people lease their UBC compute allocation to corponations on monthly contracts. Tessera's Compute Leasing Program, for example, pays 130 Quanta per month for a year-long commitment of your UBC compute allocation -- slightly above the UBC amount, locked in, guaranteed. You get a small premium. Tessera gets cheap compute at scale. The transaction feels like a fair deal. It is a fair deal in the way that selling your blood is a fair deal: you have something they want, and they are willing to pay slightly more than it costs you to replace it.

### What You Cannot Do With It

Live on it.

The UBC is calibrated to be useful enough to justify its existence and insufficient enough to ensure continued dependence on the labor market. 120 Quanta per month is precisely the amount that makes the following political argument possible: "Every citizen receives a monthly compute dividend. No one in the registered economy has zero income. The social safety net is universal, automatic, and permanent. Further welfare programs are redundant."

This argument has been used to dismantle every remaining social welfare program in every corponation territory on Earth. Public housing: redundant, UBC recipients can allocate their stipend to shelter. Public healthcare: redundant, UBC recipients can purchase medical compute time. Food assistance: redundant, UBC recipients can buy food. Education subsidies: redundant, UBC recipients can access learning platforms.

The programs were dismantled. The UBC remained. The gap between what the UBC provides and what humans need to survive became the permanent operating environment of the lower tiers.

---

## The Political Architecture

### Why It Works (As Policy)

The UBC is the most politically durable economic policy in the world because it satisfies every stakeholder's minimum requirements while serving no stakeholder's actual needs:

**Corponations** support it because it costs them almost nothing. The 120 Quanta per person per month is generated from the idle capacity of infrastructure they already own. The EDN nodes are sitting there anyway. The compute would otherwise go unused. The UBC is not a tax on profits -- it is a reallocation of waste. Total annual cost of the global UBC: approximately 11 billion Quanta, or less than 3% of Sterling-Nakamura's annual revenue alone.

**Governments** (what remains of them) support it because it eliminates the need for welfare bureaucracies they can no longer afford to operate. The Federal Remnant's social services budget dropped 94% between 2175 and 2180. The employees were not replaced. The offices were not closed -- they were repurposed as Quanta wallet registration centers.

**Political philosophers** support it (or at least cannot effectively oppose it) because it is technically universal, technically unconditional, and technically a form of ownership rather than charity. Opposing the UBC means opposing the principle that every person has a stake in the computational commons. The framing makes opposition sound like you want to take things away from people.

**The public** tolerates it because 120 Quanta is not zero. It is the difference between absolute destitution and manageable poverty. It buys three days of food. It charges your augment. It lets you ride transit to a job interview. It is not enough, and everyone knows it is not enough, and pointing out that it is not enough has become a political position without power because the response is always: "Would you prefer zero?"

### Why It Fails (As Support)

120 Quanta per month in a city where survival costs 1,200 Quanta per month is not a safety net. It is a gesture. The gap between the UBC and the cost of living is filled by:

- **Labor.** The traditional answer. Work for a corponation, earn wages, survive. The UBC ensures that the wages can be set at starvation levels because the worker already has "income."
- **Crime.** Theft, Q-jacking, salvage raids, freelance violence, data theft, organ selling. The second-largest employer in the Shelf, after corponation contract labor.
- **Informal economy.** Analog trade, barter, favors, mutual aid. The economy that exists in the gaps the Quanta system doesn't reach.
- **Compute pooling.** The one UBC-derived strategy that actually works, and the one the QFIC watches most carefully.
- **Death.** The final economic exit. Mortality rates in Tier 1 zones are 340% of Tier 3 zones. The UBC does not prevent death. It slightly delays it.

---

## The Compute Broker Economy

The UBC created an entire parasitic economy of intermediaries who profit from aggregating and reselling individual compute allocations.

**Street brokers** operate in every Shelf neighborhood. They collect UBC compute allocations from individuals -- typically purchasing monthly compute rights for 100-110 Quanta (a discount to the 120 face value) -- and resell the aggregated compute in bulk on the QCX at or near market rate. The margin is thin per transaction but enormous at scale. A broker handling 2,000 individual UBC allocations clears approximately 30,000 Quanta per month in profit.

**Compute aggregators** are larger operations -- often corponation-affiliated -- that offer structured UBC leasing programs. Tessera's program is the largest, with 4.2 million active UBC leaseholders globally. The aggregators provide the illusion of a fair market transaction: you lease your compute, they pay a premium, everyone benefits. The reality is that the aggregators capture compute at below-market rates from people who have no other option, then sell it at market rates to entities that need processing power. The spread is the business.

**Compute loan sharks** advance Quanta against future UBC allocations. Need 500 Quanta today? A compute shark will give you 500 Quanta in exchange for the next six months of your UBC compute rights. You get the money now. You get nothing for six months. If you can't survive those six months without the UBC, you borrow again. The cycle is intentional.

The QFIC has declined to regulate the compute broker market on the grounds that it represents "legitimate market activity in a voluntary exchange of property rights." The brokers are, technically, buying something you own. The fact that what you own is insufficient to keep you alive without selling it is not considered a market failure. It is considered the market working correctly.

---

## The Cruelest Kindness

The UBC's genius is that it satisfies the minimum definition of compassion while eliminating the infrastructure of actual support. Before 2175, a person in poverty could appeal to welfare systems, housing programs, food assistance, medical subsidies -- imperfect systems, underfunded systems, but systems with humans in them who could exercise judgment, make exceptions, recognize emergencies. These systems were expensive, bureaucratic, and politically vulnerable. The UBC replaced all of them with a single automated monthly deposit.

The deposit arrives on time, every time, with perfect efficiency and zero humanity.

120 Quanta. Your share of the compute. Your stake in civilization. Your proof that nobody owes you anything more, because you already received what the system determined you're worth.

In the Spires, 120 Quanta is a rounding error -- less than a cup of artisanal coffee. In the Shelf, 120 Quanta is the difference between eating on the 28th of the month and not eating on the 28th of the month. In Old Harbor, 120 Quanta doesn't arrive at all, because the people there don't have wallets, and people without wallets don't exist, and people who don't exist don't receive their share of the computational commons.

The system is complete. The system is universal. The system is fair.

The system lets children starve at a rate of 120 Quanta per month.
